newsitem.title: USA: Salomon shakes off Basis albatross.
newsitem.headline: Salomon shakes off Basis albatross.

text.p: Salomon Inc has removed a profit-bleeding thorn from its side with the sale of its Basis Petroleum Inc subsidiary, and the deal should help management to focus on core businesses this year, analysts said Monday.
"It's been a thorn in their side for a very long time," said Mark Boyar, president of Asset Analysis Focus. "It really depressed their earnings."
Leslie Nelkin, an analyst at Furman Selz, estimated Basis, which refines oil and is a wholesale marketer, was costing Salomon from $0.50 to $1 per share of profit each year.

"It should be helpful in enabling Salomon to focus on their core businesses, rather than the oil refining business," said Raphael Soifer, an analyst at Brown Brothers Harriman. Salomon's businesses include securities trading, investment banking, underwriting and other financial services.

Salomon has been aggressively seeking to unload Basis for some time, analysts said. Earlier Monday, Salomon announced that it signed a letter of intent for Valero Energy Corp to acquire the Basis unit for about $485 million.
Boyar expects that book value could jump to above $50 per share at the end of this year from the stated book of about $42 at the end of 1996, if it came close to earning what it earned last year.
Salomon earned $617 million, or $4.84 per diluted share in 1996, versus $457 million, or $3.50 in 1995.

"We think earnings power for Salomon has increased as a direct result of the sale of Basis," Boyar said. He feels Salomon has peak earnings power of $8 per share, without the refining business, should Wall Street overall have a good year. Nelkin estimated earnings of about $7 for this year.

Nelkin sees Salomon improving performance in its growing financial services business, in part due to its alliance with mutual fund giant Fidelity Investments. "It gives Salomon some retail power, which it did not previously have," he said.
Nelkin expects that while it will not likely match the 22 percent return on equity rate of 1996, "it's not unreasonable for them to generate a ROE in the high teens" this year.
Salomon's Phibro unit, which trades grains, natural gas, and oil, continues to fit more with the main business, said Richard Strauss, an analyst at Goldman Sachs.
"It's something they've made money in consistently," said Strauss. "It's counter-cyclical revenue," when interest rates rise and the stock market suffers a downturn.
Valero will acquire the stock of Basis for $285 million, plus approximately $200 million for inventories and other working capital to be acquired in the transaction.
Salomon said it will restate fourth quarter results to a net loss of $62 million, or $0.71 per share, to reflect an aftertax loss of $290 million from the Basis sale.
